title: Design for Performance in Architecture
overview: This topic covers how to define, measure and design for performance in an architecture. It builds from the core metrics (response time, throughput, utilization, load) through queueing theory and its laws (utilization, forced flow, Little's, general response time, M/M/1 and multi-server models) to tactics such as load balancing, caching, precomputation and flow control, and finally validation by modelling, prototyping and documentation. In the exam expect numeric questions using these formulas plus scenarios asking you to find bottlenecks and justify tactics.
big_ideas: Response time includes service, queueing and communication within a stated boundary. Serial visit times add; concurrent branches that must all finish contribute their maximum plus coordination overhead.
Serial pipeline **capacity** is limited by the bottleneck. Independent load-balanced replicas can add capacity when work is distributed and no shared bottleneck intervenes.
For a stable single resource, utilization U = X S, where X is its throughput; if no work is lost, X equals arrival rate λ. Forced flow accounts for repeated visits: X_i = X_0 V_i.
Little's Law n = λR; General Response Time Law R = sum of R_i V_i.
M/M/1: R = S/(1-U) = 1/(µ-λ); response time explodes as utilization nears 100%, so keep utilization below the knee.
Shared-queue M/M/c and separate c(M/M/1) use different models. Both require per-server utilization ρ = λS/c < 1; the lecture’s M/M/c response-time formula is approximate.
Tactics: control demand, manage resources, load balance, cache (weighted hit/miss), precompute, lower algorithmic complexity, remove bottlenecks.
Validate early by simulation and prototyping; document major components, big messages and high-frequency calls.

sections.title: What performance means: the core metrics
sections.summary: Performance is useful work done accurately, efficiently and quickly, and it is judged through a handful of metrics: response time, throughput, utilization, load, latency and think time.

items: Specify **response time**, **throughput** and **resource use**
...for a **stated workload**
**Low utilization alone is not proof** of good performance: an idle system may simply be doing little work
**Use metrics together**

notes.lead: **Response time = service time + waiting time + transmission time**
items: **Service time**: how long the work itself takes
**Waiting (queue) time**: how long the request sits behind others
**Transmission time**: moving the request and reply
notes.foot: For finer analysis each piece can be split further (**network**, **rendering**, **processing**).

items: **Throughput** = rate of **completed** work; **load** = rate of **incoming** work
**Arrival rate** (input rate, load) → counts requests coming in per period
**Response rate** (output rate, throughput) → counts responses going out
**Throughput is a better indicator** of system performance than **clock speed** or **disk seek time**, because it reflects all components together
**Utilization = used capacity / total capacity**
= the **share of time a component is busy**
**Busy CPU or disk** cannot take other work → pending requests wait
**High utilization is what creates queueing**
May mean **request rate**, **throughput** or **utilization**: write the **units**
**Stable, loss-free system** → arrival and completion rates match
**End-to-end latency** vs **network latency** are different boundaries: specify which is being measured
**Think time** = the user's pause between actions
Does **not** measure the system
But it **changes utilization and throughput calculations**
→ matters for **performance testing** and **capacity planning**

terms.def: Elapsed time from a request until its response: service + waiting + transmission.
Number of responses completed per unit time (output rate).
Used capacity divided by total capacity; share of time busy.
Minimum time to send data from one component to another.
Time a user spends between successive actions.

check.q: A vendor offers a server with a 30% faster CPU clock. Your application spends 70% of each request waiting on the database. Will throughput rise by 30%?
check.a: No. Throughput reflects the whole system, and here the database dominates, so a faster CPU speeds up only the small CPU share of the work. Measure throughput under your own workload before paying for clock speed. Upgrading the bottleneck resource (the database, or how it is used) is what raises throughput.

check.q: A dashboard shows CPU at 20%, and the team concludes performance is fine. Users report 8-second responses. What is wrong with the conclusion?
check.a: Low utilisation is not proof of good performance. The time may be spent waiting on another resource (database locks, disk, a slow dependency, the network), or the CPU may be idle because work is stuck elsewhere. Look at response time, throughput and the utilisation of each resource together to find where the time goes.

check.q: A load test fires requests back-to-back from 500 virtual users with zero think time. Real users pause about 10 s between actions, and responses take about 1 s. What does the test misrepresent?
check.a: The load. With no think time, 500 users generate about 500 requests/s; with a 10 s pause they generate about 500 / (10 + 1), roughly 45 requests/s. The test therefore models a far heavier load than 500 real users. Set realistic think times and arrival rates, or the results won't map to the requirement.

check.q: Average response time rose from 300 ms to 2 s while service time stayed at 250 ms. Where did the extra time go, and how would you confirm it?
check.a: Response time is service time plus waiting time plus transmission time. With service unchanged, the growth is almost certainly waiting in queues caused by higher utilisation, or possibly transmission. Confirm by checking queue lengths, utilisation and network timings at each tier.

sections.title: Combining components: serial vs parallel, load vs throughput
sections.summary: How response time and throughput combine across components in series and in parallel, how throughput saturates as load grows, and worked exercises on a burger shop, a game server and a four-tier stack.

items: **Add response times** along the request path
**Pipeline capacity** is **limited by the lowest stage capacity** (when each request visits each stage once)
**Repeated visits** → compare **service demand per system request** instead
**Concurrent branches of one request** → contribute their **maximum time** when all results are required
**Load-balanced replicas** → process **different requests** and can **add capacity**
Include **coordination overhead** where relevant
**1 minute** to prepare + **0.5 minute** to pack = **1.5 minutes** of work
→ capacity **40 burgers/hour**
**Halving that service time doubles this worker’s capacity**
notes.foot: This does **not** establish that any reduction in end-to-end response time doubles system throughput.

items: **Below saturation**: a stable system completing one response per accepted request → **throughput = arrival rate**
Capacity **20/s**, arrivals **22/s** → completion rate **cannot exceed 20/s**; the excess **queues or is rejected**
**At or above capacity**: an **unbounded queue** has **no finite steady-state waiting time**
**Ideal**: throughput rises **linearly** then **flattens at capacity**
**Real interactive systems fall short** of the ideal curve: **co-ordination overhead** keeps them below that ceiling
**Congestion penalty** → a badly behaved system's throughput actually **falls** as load keeps increasing

notes.lead: **1000 players**, each waits **3 seconds** after a response.
items: **50 ms** server time, **200 ms** round-trip network time
Assumes **enough parallel capacity**, **no queueing**, **one outstanding request per player**
If response time **already includes network time**, do **not add latency again**
**Reverse proxy**: 10+90 = **100 ms**
**Sum 1080 ms** + **200 ms network latency** = **1280 ms**
**Throughput** (one server per tier) = **min(10, 16, 6, 20) = 6 tps**, set by the **app server**

terms.def: Required stages on a request path: add visit times; the capacity bottleneck limits throughput.
Concurrent branches or replicated workers; identify which before combining times or capacities.
Point at which load reaches maximum throughput; extra load only queues.

check.q: Three tiers in series take 50, 100 and 600 ms per request and have capacities of 40, 12 and 25 requests/s. Which tier do you work on to cut response time, and which to raise throughput?
check.a: For response time, the 600 ms tier, which is the largest share of the 750 ms total. For throughput, the 12 requests/s tier, which caps the pipeline. They are different tiers: the biggest contributor to response time is not necessarily the capacity bottleneck, so measure both.

check.q: Four tiers have throughputs 10, 16, 6 and 20 tps in series. What is system throughput, and what happens if you double the DB?
check.a: System throughput is min = 6 tps (app server). Doubling the DB changes nothing because the app server remains the bottleneck.

check.q: A system can complete at most 20 requests/s and receives 22/s for an hour. What happens to throughput and response time?
check.a: Throughput stays at 20/s, its capacity. The excess 2 requests/s either queue or are rejected. With an unbounded queue, about 7,200 requests are waiting after an hour, and response time keeps climbing with no steady state. Add capacity or shed or throttle load; waiting it out does not help.

check.q: A page calls three services in parallel, taking 120, 300 and 80 ms, and needs all three results. A teammate estimates 500 ms for the page. Do you agree?
check.a: No. Branches that run concurrently contribute their maximum, so the page takes about 300 ms plus coordination overhead. The 300 ms service is the one to speed up; improving the other two changes nothing. If the calls were sequential, the teammate's sum would be right.

Lowest stage capacity for one visit each

sections.title: Queueing theory notation and the operational laws
sections.summary: Queueing theory models jobs, servers and waiting; the operational laws (utilization, forced flow, bottleneck) hold on observed measurements regardless of distribution.

items: **Queueing theory** = mathematical basis for **response time**, **throughput** and **utilization**
→ and so for **performance analysis** and **capacity planning**
A **population** generates **arrivals at rate λ** → jobs **wait** → **c servers** each take **service time S**
**Jobs in the system = jobs in queue + jobs in service**
**λ**: arrival rate
**S**: mean service time
**µ = 1/S**: per-server service capacity
**X**: actual throughput
**c**: server count
**ρ = λ/(cµ)**: mean utilization per identical server under stable, balanced load
**L/L_q**: count jobs in system/queue; **W/W_q**: their residence/wait times
**P_n**: probability of n jobs; **K**: the capacity limit
**Operational laws are measurement identities**: independent of arrival and service distributions
Keep **units**, **observation interval** and **system boundary** consistent; **account for losses**
**Queueing-model predictions** need extra assumptions: **steady state**, **exponential service**, **Poisson arrivals**
**U = X S** for one service resource
**Stable loss-free system**: X = λ → **U = λS = λ/µ**
Example: **20 orders/hour x 1.5 minutes/order** = 30 busy minutes/hour = **50%**
Example: **125 packets/s x 0.002 s** = **25%**
A **component's load** = **system load x its visit ratio V_i**
**V_i** = average visits to it per system request
**D_i = V_i S_i**
Single resources: **U_i = X_0 D_i** → the **highest demand saturates first** (bottleneck)
Component with **c_i equivalent parallel workers** → compare **D_i/c_i** and **effective capacity** instead
Do **not ignore different worker counts**

notes.lead: Each instruction needs **5 s of CPU**, **80 I/Os to storage A (50 ms each)**, **100 I/Os to storage B (30 ms each)**; storage A throughput observed as **15.70/s**.
items: → the **CPU is the bottleneck**

terms.def: Mean arrival rate of requests.
Mean service capacity of one server, 1/S; actual throughput can be lower.
Average number of visits to component i per system request.
V_i x S_i: total service time component i spends per system request.

check.q: Each request uses 40 ms of application CPU and makes 3 database calls of 20 ms each. At 15 requests/s, which resource saturates first, and at what request rate?
check.a: Service demand: CPU 40 ms, database 3 x 20 = 60 ms. At 15 requests/s, the database is 15 x 0.06 = 90% busy and the CPU 60%. The database saturates first, at 1 / 0.06, about 16.7 requests/s. Cutting database visits per request (for example by batching or caching) raises that limit more than a faster CPU would.

check.q: A gateway forwards 125 packets/s, taking 2 ms each. What is its utilisation, and at what rate does it saturate?
check.a: U = 125 x 0.002 = 25%. It saturates at 1 / 0.002 = 500 packets/s. Response time will rise sharply well before that point because of queueing, so don't plan to run it near 100%.

check.q: A colleague says you cannot apply the Utilization Law because the arrivals are bursty, not Poisson. Do you agree?
check.a: No. The operational laws are identities over measured quantities: U = XS holds for the observed interval, whatever the arrival distribution. What does need distribution assumptions is predicting queueing delay, as in M/M/1. Keep the units, interval and system boundary consistent.

visuals.title: Operational laws
rows: U = X S; X = λ if stable and loss-free
Busy share = completions per time x service per completion
Component load = system load x visits per request
U_i = λ_0 V_i S_i = λ_0 D_i
Highest D_i saturates first for equal single-resource capacity
λ_0 = 0.196 job/s; CPU is the bottleneck

sections.title: Little's Law and the General Response Time Law
sections.summary: Little's Law links jobs in the system to arrival rate and response time; the General Response Time Law sums component times weighted by visits.

items: For **stable long-run averages** with **consistent boundaries**
**n** counts requests both **waiting and in service**
**R** includes **all time within that same boundary**
Use the **accepted arrival/completion rate**; **account for rejected work**
**15 customers/hour = 0.25/min**
**1.6 burgers/customer** x **1.5 minutes/burger** = **2.4 minutes** of work
→ **n = 0.6 customers** **if queueing is ignored**
With **measured waiting**, add it to **residence time** before using Little’s Law
notes.foot: **Service time is not generally total time in the shop.**

notes.h: Little's Law backwards: component response times
items: Observed jobs **n = 8.88, 3.19, 1.40** at CPU, A and B
**R = sum over i=1..M of R_i V_i**
Total response time = sum of each component's **response time per visit x its visits**
Equivalently **13.47 jobs / 0.196 job/s** via Little's Law

terms.def: n = λR: jobs in system = arrival rate x response time.
R = sum of R_i V_i over all M components.

check.q: A server has a pool of 40 threads. Requests arrive at 100/s and spend 0.3 s each in the server. Is the pool big enough, and what if a slow dependency raises the time to 0.6 s?
check.a: By Little's Law, n = 100 x 0.3 = 30 requests in the server, which fits within 40 threads. At 0.6 s, n = 60, more than the pool: requests queue for threads, response time climbs further, and the failure can cascade upstream. A timeout on the dependency, or a larger pool, protects against this.

check.q: Measured per-visit response times: CPU 0.25 s over 181 visits, storage A 0.203 s over 80 visits, storage B 0.071 s over 100 visits. Which contributes most to the 68.6 s job time, and what does that suggest?
check.a: By the General Response Time Law: CPU 0.25 x 181, about 45.3 s; A 0.203 x 80, about 16.2 s; B 0.071 x 100, about 7.1 s. The CPU dominates, mostly because of its visit count. Reduce the CPU's visits or its per-visit time before tuning storage.

check.q: A shop serves 15 customers an hour, and you observe an average of 3 customers inside. How long does a customer spend in the shop?
check.a: R = n / λ = 3 / 0.25 per minute = 12 minutes. That includes both waiting and service, because n counted everyone inside. Use the same boundary for n and R.

visuals.title: Keep one boundary for Little’s Law

steps.label: Accepted arrivals
steps.detail: Count requests entering the chosen system. Excluded or rejected requests must not inflate the accepted arrival rate.

steps.label: Inside the system
steps.detail: Include both waiting and processing within this boundary: n = 50 x 0.2 = 10 requests on average.

steps.label: Completed responses
steps.detail: At steady state without loss, completions match arrivals. Network time belongs in R only if the network is inside the chosen boundary.

sections.title: Queues and the M/M/1 response time curve
sections.summary: Even when average capacity exceeds average load, random or bursty arrivals create queues; M/M/1 gives response time as S/(1-U), which explodes as utilization nears 100%.

items: **Burger shop**: a customer every **2 min** on average, service **1.5 min** → **U = 75%**
Yet arrivals are **random and bursty** (e.g. **30 customers in the last 5 minutes** after **55 idle minutes**) → queues form
notes.foot: **Averages hide bursts**, which is why **queueing models** are needed.

items: Specifies **arrival distribution**, **service distribution**, **servers**, **capacity**, **population** and **discipline**
**M** = Markovian assumptions; **D** = deterministic; **Ek** = Erlang; **G** = general; **PH** = phase-type
**Disciplines**: FIFO, LIFO, round robin, processor sharing, priority

sub: one shared queue feeding c servers

items: Assumes **Poisson arrivals** and **independent exponential service times**
**One server**, stable rate **λ < µ**
**Mean response R = S/(1-U) = 1/(µ-λ)**
Example: **20 orders/hour**, capacity **30/hour** → **S = 2 minutes**, **U = 2/3**, **R = 6 minutes** (including **4 minutes waiting**)
**50%** utilization → **R = 2 seconds**
notes.foot: These are **model outputs**, not a **universal safe-utilization threshold**. Use the **workload**, **measured curve** and **response target** to choose **headroom**.

notes.lead: **U_i = λ_0 V_i S_i**; with the same arrival rate:
items: Lower **S_i** → **faster service**
Lower **V_i** → **fewer visits**
Or **reduce the arrival rate** to the system → **throttling**, **spreading load**

terms.def: One-server queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service; steady-state formulas need λ < µ.
A/B/C/K/N/D: arrival, service, servers, capacity, population, discipline.
Utilization/load at which response time starts to climb sharply.

check.q: Orders arrive at 20 an hour, and one server completes 30 an hour, giving a 6-minute average time in system. The target is under 3 minutes. Would a server that completes 45 an hour meet it?
check.a: Yes. Under M/M/1, R = 1 / (µ - λ) = 1 / (45 - 20) hours = 2.4 minutes. Utilisation falls from 67% to 44%, which is where the waiting time goes. This assumes random (Poisson) arrivals and exponential service, so validate with measured data.

check.q: Average utilization is 75%, so why is there still a queue?
check.a: Arrivals are random and bursty. A burst of jobs arrives faster than the server can handle even though the average load is below capacity, so waiting occurs; response time rises as 1/(1 - U).

check.q: To save money, a team plans to run its application servers at 90% CPU. Service time is 1 s, and the response target is 3 s. Under M/M/1, is the plan safe?
check.a: No. R = S / (1 - U) gives 10 s at 90%, far over target. Meeting 3 s needs U of 2/3 or less (1 / (1 - 0.67) = 3). Size the headroom from the response target and measured workload; there is no universally safe percentage.

check.q: Arrivals and service capacity are both 30 requests/hour. Can M/M/1 predict a finite mean response time?
check.a: No. U = 1, so the steady-state denominator µ - λ is zero. The model requires λ < µ; equality leaves no spare capacity to drain random bursts.

sections.title: Multiple servers, queue layouts and price/performance
sections.summary: Compare faster single server, parallel queues and one shared queue; plus how to size servers for a target and measure price/performance.

items: **a = λS** = **offered load**; **ρ = a/c** = utilization per identical server
**Balanced separate M/M/1 queues** → **R = S/(1-ρ)**
**One shared M/M/c queue** → lecture approximation **R ≈ S/(1-ρ^c)**; the **appendix gives exact Erlang C**
Require **ρ < 1**
**Offered load a can exceed 1**; an **individual server’s utilization cannot**

notes.lead: **2 customers/min**, **S = 1.5 min**, target **queueing time under 3 min**.
items: **Offered load a = 2 x 1.5 = 3** → **ρ = 3/c**; target **R < S + 3 = 4.5 min**
notes.foot: The deck leaves these as **exercises**; these numbers apply its formulas.

items: For **identical workers** under the lecture’s queue assumptions
**Shared queue** avoids **idle workers** while another queue has waiting jobs → **lower response** than separate queues
**Not a guarantee** for **specialised jobs** or **real distributed systems**
**Additional workers move the saturation point**
But response still **rises sharply** as per-server utilization approaches **100%**
**Size for the response target** and required **failure headroom**, not just the **minimum stable server count**
**Price/performance = cost / throughput** (e.g. **$/tps**)
**TPC benchmarks** use **price per transaction**

items.t: **Google's cluster design** → chose **cheap mid-range PC-like servers**
sub: = (**capital expense with depreciation** plus **operating costs**) divided by **performance**
expecting a server to last only **2-3 years**

items: **Response = waiting + service**
**Capacity** limits **sustainable throughput**
**Arrival rate** determines throughput **below that limit**
notes.foot: A **quicker response does not necessarily increase throughput** when demand is unchanged.

terms.def: Per-server utilization ρ = λS/c for identical workers; steady-state queue formulas require ρ < 1.
c servers, each with its own queue.
c servers sharing one queue.
Cost divided by throughput, e.g. $ per tps or cost per query.

check.q: A bank branch has 4 tellers. Should each teller have their own line, or should one shared line feed all four?
check.a: One shared line. With identical tellers, a free teller always takes the next customer, whereas separate lines can leave one teller idle while another line waits. This assumes every teller can serve every customer; specialised counters change the comparison.

check.q: You need to triple capacity: one server three times faster, or three servers? Give the performance answer and the availability answer.
check.a: For response time, the lecture's ideal model favours one fast server, then three servers sharing a queue, then three separate queues. For availability, the single fast server is a single point of failure, while three servers survive one loss. Most production systems accept slightly higher response time for that redundancy.

check.q: A sizing target says 'queueing below 3 minutes', and service takes 1.5 minutes. What response-time limit should you test?
check.a: R = waiting + service, so require R < 4.5 minutes. Comparing a response-time formula directly with 3 minutes would impose a different, stricter target.

check.q: Server A costs $10,000 and delivers 500 tps. Server B costs $3,000 and delivers 120 tps. Which has better price/performance, and what else would you check?
check.a: A: $20 per tps; B: $25 per tps, so A is better on capital cost. Also check operating costs and expected lifetime (Google counted both when choosing commodity servers), the impact of losing one large server versus one small one, and whether the load comes in steps that suit smaller units.

sections.title: Performance tactics and load balancing
sections.summary: The tactic families (control demand, manage resources) and design heuristics, then how load balancing improves throughput and speed and its state problem.

items: **Apply tactics**
**Validate by performance modelling**
**Validate by prototyping**
**Load balancing**
**Caching**
**Pre-computation**
**Reduce algorithmic complexity**
**Avoid or reduce bottlenecks** (may **trade off with cost**)
**Distributes requests across instances**
**Lowers queueing** when it uses **spare capacity** effectively
Need **not reduce a request’s own processing time**
**Splitting one job into independent parallel subtasks** is a separate way to **reduce service time**
**Round robin**
**Random**
**Server load**
**Least response time**
**Traffic served**
**Number of active connections**
**Geographic location**
**Capabilities**
notes.foot: **Policy choice matters** because **uneven or blind distribution** leaves some servers **hot**.

items: Server holds **client state** (e.g. a **session**) → client must keep returning to that server (**sticky**)
Otherwise **state must be externalized**

terms.def: Distributing requests across multiple servers to improve throughput, speed and availability.
Routing a client always to the server that holds its session state.

check.q: Adding a second server behind a load balancer halved average response time, although each request's processing time did not change. Why?
check.a: Each server's utilisation roughly halved, so requests spend far less time waiting in queues; response time is waiting plus service. The service time is unchanged. To cut it, you would need faster processing or parallel work within the request itself.

check.q: A load balancer uses least-connections with sticky sessions. After a campaign, one server holds 60% of active users and is overloaded. Diagnose it and fix it.
check.a: Stickiness overrides the balancing policy: users stay pinned to the server that first held their session. Move session state out of the servers into a shared store so any server can take any request. The cost is a network hop to the state store.

check.q: A partner's month-end batch job floods the system with requests, and interactive users time out. Which tactic family applies, and what would you do?
check.a: Control resource demand: manage the arrival rate (throttle the partner) and prioritise input, so interactive requests go ahead of batch. The batch job takes longer as a result. Adding resources would also work, but costs more for a predictable monthly peak.

check.q: Servers of different sizes (8 and 32 cores) sit behind a round-robin load balancer, and the small ones are overloaded. What would you change?
check.a: Round robin ignores capability, so the 8-core servers get the same share as the 32-core ones. Use a capability-weighted or server-load policy, or least response time, so work follows actual capacity.

sections.title: Caching and precomputation
sections.summary: Caches trade extra storage for faster access; their value depends on hit ratio, relative access times and cost, and precomputation applies the same idea to computed results.

items: **Cache** stores data for **faster access**
**Hit** → finds the data in cache
**Miss** → goes to the source; costs **cache lookup + source access**

notes.lead: **Weighted average over hits and misses.** Cache **5 ms**, data source **50 ms**:
items: vs **50 ms** with no cache → **worth it**
**Break-even** for this hit ratio = cache access time of **10 ms** (5 + 0.8 x 50 = 45; **10 + 0.8 x 50 = 50**)
Above that → **the cache hurts**
**Fast storage is expensive**, hence **small**
**Location**: local machine, local network, near or far remote
**Operation**: simple **primary-key lookup** vs **complex query**
Consider **storage and bandwidth** vs **response or throughput gain**
With **only 15 GB**: use **partial-cache hit-rate measurements** before assuming B retains that **average benefit** or **allocating all space** to it
Assumes **equal-sized items** kept in **popularity order**
**Power-law distribution** → favours caching a **small hot set**
**Uniform access** → roughly **proportional benefit**
Lecture’s “**half the cache gives at least half the hits**” relies on these assumptions, **not every eviction policy** or **changing workload**
**Trades write/computation cost for cheaper reads**
Lecture’s **historical Twitter example**: **timeline reads (~300k/s)** vs **posts (4.6k–12k/s)**
**Fan-out-on-write** → prebuilds follower timelines
**Fan-out-on-read** → computes at **viewing time**
**Hybrid** → avoids writing to every follower’s cache for **celebrity posts**
notes.foot: These figures **illustrate the design**, not current traffic.

terms.def: Requested data is / is not found in the cache.
Computing results ahead of time and storing them for later use.
Benefit per unit of cache used; ranks what to cache first.

check.q: Cache access takes 8 ms, the source takes 50 ms, and the hit ratio is 20%. Is the cache worth it? If cache access were 15 ms, what hit ratio would you need?
check.a: At 8 ms: 0.2 x 8 + 0.8 x (8 + 50) = 48 ms against 50 ms without the cache, a small gain. At 15 ms, the expected time is 15 + (1 - h) x 50, which must be under 50, so h must exceed 30%. Below that, the cache adds cost and latency.

check.q: A social app's feed reads outnumber posts 50 to 1, and one account has 20 million followers. Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or a hybrid?
check.a: A hybrid. Fan-out on write precomputes timelines, so the dominant reads are cheap. For the 20-million-follower account, writing to every follower's timeline on each post is too costly, so merge its posts in at read time. The trade-off is extra read-time work for followers of such accounts, as in the lecture's Twitter example.

check.q: With 15 GB of cache and data types A (10 GB, 10 ms), B (20 GB, 30 ms), C (30 GB, 10 ms), what do you cache?
check.a: The full-cache average benefit/GB ranks B, A, C, but B needs 20 GB for its measured 30 ms gain. With only 15 GB, measure partial hit ratios and marginal benefits, then allocate the available space. The full-cache ratios alone do not prove the best split.

check.q: A product catalogue has 1 million items. In shop X, access is spread evenly across them; in shop Y, it follows a power law. A cache holds 1% of the items. Where does it help?
check.a: In shop Y: under a power law, a small set of popular items gets most of the requests, so 1% of items can yield a high hit ratio. In shop X, access is uniform, so a 1% cache gives roughly a 1% hit ratio, which is not worth it. Measure the access distribution before sizing a cache.

sections.title: Algorithmic complexity, data placement and flow control
sections.summary: Reduce work growth with better algorithms, put computation where data movement is smallest, optimise storage, and control flow to protect shared resources.

items: **Big O describes growth**, not exact seconds (ignoring constants)
**O(1)** → stays bounded
**O(n)** → grows **tenfold** for **10x input**
**O(n^2)** → grows **hundredfold**
**Compare algorithms at the expected data size**; **constants**, **memory** and **I/O** still affect measured performance

notes.h: Where code runs changes network cost
notes.lead: **Job-candidate matching** case: **score every pair**, return the **top 1000**.
items: Scoring in the **app server** → pulls **all the data across the network**
Pushing it into the **database server** → transfers **only results**
Weigh growth in **scoring operations** (**time complexity**) vs growth in **network transfers**
**Reads and writes to storage** are often **the bottleneck**
The **right index** helps greatly
The **right storage technology** matters too → e.g. a **graph database** for **relationship-heavy data** like **social networks**

sub: a **customer ordering 25 packets** ahead of you
a **burger shop with 5 staff** and **20 sudden customers**

items: Motivate **limiting rates**
**Fair queueing**
**Separate lanes or roles**
notes.foot: So **one demanding user or burst cannot starve others**.

terms.def: Notation for how time or space grows with input size.
Limiting or shaping request flow so one source or burst cannot overload shared resources.

check.q: A matching job takes 2 s for 10,000 candidates using an O(n^2) algorithm. Data will grow to 100,000. Would you buy 10x hardware or change the algorithm?
check.a: O(n^2) means 100 times the work, about 200 s. Even with 10x hardware that scales perfectly, it still takes about 20 s, and every further growth repeats the problem. An O(n log n) algorithm grows only about 12.5 times for 10 times the data. Change the algorithm, and verify with measurements at the expected size, because constants and I/O also matter.

check.q: Scoring every candidate-job pair currently happens in the application server, which pulls all the rows over the network to return the top 1,000. When should the scoring move into the database server?
check.a: When the data volume is large and the result small, as here: running it in the database transfers only 1,000 results instead of every row. The trade-off is load on the database server, which is usually harder to scale, so check its spare capacity first.

check.q: A 'friends of friends within 3 hops' query on a relational store takes 9 seconds. What would you investigate?
check.a: The data store, which is often the bottleneck: first the indexes on the relationship tables, then whether the storage technology fits. Relationship-heavy traversals like this suit a graph database. Switching stores is costly, so prove the gain with a prototype first.

check.q: One API customer sends 25 large requests at once, and everyone else's requests wait behind them. What would you add?
check.a: Flow control: per-client rate limits, plus fair queueing or separate lanes, so one demanding client or burst cannot starve the others. That customer's batch then takes longer, which you can offer as a paid higher limit if it matters.

sections.title: Validating the design and documenting performance
sections.summary: Use simulation, prototyping and benchmarking to verify performance early, and document performance-relevant parts of the architecture at the right level.

items: **Queue-modelling simulators** (e.g. the **open source JMT**) → test how a design will behave
**Prototyping and benchmarking** → check the architecture **meets targets before the whole system is built**
**Fail early**, especially with **unknown technology** or **experimental design**
**Define goals**
**Identify the extent** of prototyping needed
**Build the prototype** (possibly with **instrumentation**)
**Benchmark**
**Repeat** until **performance risk is contained**
notes.foot: Trade-off: **level of confidence vs effort and cost**.

items: **Block diagram** → **components**, e.g. **service layer** between **front-end channels** and **back-end systems**
**Sequence diagram** → **calls in order**, **loops** such as repeated **back-end transform/send** steps
**Data flow diagram** → **messages**, **encoded vs decoded**, **audit logs**

notes.h: Document what matters: sweet spot of detail
items: **Not too high-level, not too low-level**
**Analyze related data together**: one architecture may face **heavy online transactions** and **timely complex reporting**
**Pick a viewpoint, draw and iterate**; **granularity varies by viewpoint**
**One outstanding request per client** → **average request rate = clients / (think time + end-to-end response time)**
Add **network latency separately** only when **excluded from response time**
**Exact M/M/c** uses **Erlang C** for the **probability an arrival must wait**
The **main lecture formula is an approximation**

terms.def: Measuring a prototype or system against defined performance goals.
Probability that all servers are busy so an arriving request must queue.

check.q: A team will adopt a message broker none of them has used, with a target of 2,000 messages/s at peak. What would you do before the full build?
check.a: Prototype and benchmark it: set the goal (2,000 messages/s at the required latency), decide how much to build, instrument it, run it at the target load, and repeat until the risk is contained. Unknown technology is exactly where you should fail early. The trade-off is confidence against prototyping effort.

check.q: Two developers time the search API from home with a browser tool and get 0.8 s and 4 s. Why are the results unreliable, and how would you test properly?
check.a: The client, network and load are uncontrolled, and each person sends a handful of requests, so the numbers reflect their connections, not the system under its required load. Use a scripted load test from a controlled environment, with a defined arrival rate, think time and request mix, and report percentiles against the target. A queueing model or simulation can complement it.

check.q: A performance document shows only one box diagram: front end, service layer, back ends. What is missing?
check.a: The performance-relevant detail: a sequence diagram showing call order and loops, such as repeated back-end calls per request, and a data flow showing large messages, calls that carry many records, and high-frequency interactions. Aim for the level of detail where these become visible, without drawing every class.

steps.label: Define goals
steps.detail: State the performance targets to verify.

steps.label: Scope prototype
steps.detail: Decide how much to prototype to meet those goals.

steps.label: Build
steps.detail: Build the prototype, possibly instrumented for measurement.

steps.label: Benchmark
steps.detail: Run benchmarks and loop until the performance risk is contained.

exam_angles.q: A request passes a firewall (5 ms wait, 45 ms service, 10 tps capacity), a reverse proxy (10, 90, 16 tps), an app server (50, 550, 6 tps) and a database (30, 300, 20 tps), with 200 ms of network latency. (a) Find the response time and throughput. (b) You add a second app server. What is the new throughput, and what is the next bottleneck?
exam_angles.a: (a) Response time = 50 + 100 + 600 + 330 = 1080 ms, plus 200 ms latency, giving 1280 ms. Throughput = min(10, 16, 6, 20) = 6 tps, limited by the app server. (b) Two app servers give about 12 tps, so throughput becomes min(10, 16, 12, 20) = 10 tps, and the firewall is now the bottleneck. Each request's service time is unchanged, so response time improves only through less queueing at the app tier. To go beyond 10 tps, scale the firewall as well.

exam_angles.q: Each job needs 5 s of CPU, 80 I/Os on storage A (50 ms each) and 100 I/Os on storage B (30 ms each). Storage A is observed at 15.70 I/Os per second. Find the system throughput, the utilisations and the bottleneck. What would it take to double throughput?
exam_angles.a: Forced Flow: λ_0 = 15.70 / 80 = 0.196 jobs/s. Demands: CPU 5 s, A 4 s, B 3 s. U = λ_0 x D gives CPU 98%, A 78.4%, B 58.8%; the CPU is the bottleneck, and maximum throughput is 1 / 5 = 0.2 jobs/s. To double to about 0.39 jobs/s, every demand must fall below about 2.56 s. Halving CPU demand alone leaves A as the limit at 1 / 4 = 0.25 jobs/s, so storage A, and storage B (3 s), also need faster devices, fewer visits or more parallel units. Bottlenecks move as you fix them.

exam_angles.q: A shop receives 20 requests an hour, and one server handles 30 an hour. Compute the utilisation and average time in system. Then, at 2 requests per minute with a 1.5-minute service time and a target of queueing under 3 minutes, a faster server is not possible: how many servers do you need with separate queues, and with one shared queue?
exam_angles.a: For 20/hour arrivals and 30/hour capacity, U = 2/3 and R = 6 minutes including service. For λ = 2/min and S = 1.5 minutes, the offered load is 3, so ρ = 3/c. Waiting under 3 minutes means R < 4.5. Separate queues need c = 5; the lecture's approximate shared-queue model gives c = 4. Both need ρ < 1. Validate the chosen model with measured data and add headroom for a server failure.

exam_angles.q: 1000 players each trigger an event every 3 s (think time). Server time is 50 ms and the round trip is 200 ms. What load must the server handle, and how many requests are in flight?
exam_angles.a: Assuming one outstanding request per player and no queueing, the rate is 1000 / (3 + 0.05 + 0.2) = 307.7/s. Work in the server averages 307.7 x 0.05 = 15.4 requests. Including network time, 307.7 x 0.25 = 76.9 requests are in flight. State the boundary you are counting; the remaining players are thinking.

exam_angles.q: A product-detail lookup takes 50 ms from the database. A cache would take 5 ms. Measured access is uniform across the catalogue, and a cache the size you can afford gives a 20% hit ratio. A teammate says to add the cache. Argue for or against, and say what would change your mind.
exam_angles.a: Expected time = 0.2 x 5 + 0.8 x 55 = 45 ms against 50 ms: a 10% gain for the cost of the cache memory and an extra component, which is weak. It stops paying at all if cache access reaches 10 ms or the hit ratio falls. With uniform access, a larger cache raises hits only in proportion to its size. What would change the decision: a power-law access pattern, where a small cache catches most requests; precomputing the expensive part of the page; or a source that is much slower than 50 ms. Measure before buying.

exam_angles.q: A web tier runs at 85% utilisation with 4 s average response time against a 2 s target, and 40% of requests fetch the same home-page data. Which tactics would you apply, in what order, and how would you verify them before building?
exam_angles.a: First reduce demand: cache or precompute the home-page data, removing up to 40% of the work and lowering utilisation and queueing. Then manage resources: add servers behind a load balancer (shared queue) so per-server utilisation falls well below 85%, and fix any algorithmic or database bottleneck the measurements show. If needed, throttle or deprioritise non-interactive load. Verify with a queueing model or simulation (for example JMT) and an instrumented prototype benchmark under the real request mix, repeating until the 2 s target holds with headroom.
